summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights wishes was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment; it does not establish a right that a visitor can invoke at a border or before a local court.

Senior Curaçao officials have publicly endorsed equal treatment. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano backed "equal rights for everyone" in the local press.

Enforcement practice has not consistently followed that rhetoric. Winifred Raveneau, a Pueblo Soberano party colleague of Wiels, opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT "Pink House" centre in 2010 and, alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten, has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom.
tangentialFactors:
Curaçao's international reputation runs ahead of its permitting record. Frank Holtslag of Curaçao Gay Pride cites the island's IGLTA award as naming it the most gay-welcoming destination in the region, and a travel-press profile updated January 2017 describes the ABC islands as quiet nests of gay-friendliness. Both are promotional or editorial characterisations rather than assessments of legal exposure.

Regional comparison: Aruba, a sibling constituent country of the Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That statute governs Aruba, not Curaçao, and nothing in these sources establishes an equivalent partner-recognition measure in Curaçao itself.

The 2015 equal-rights agreement was pursued through a package of wishes delivered to ministers in The Hague, a diplomatic route that carries no automatic effect in local courts or at the border.
localsOnly:
Residents organise through the Pink House centre, opened in 2010 as an LGBT hub and cited in travel-press coverage of the island.

Event approvals depend on party-level positions rather than settled administrative practice. Pueblo Soberano supplied both the commissioner who endorsed equal rights in 2015 and the party colleague whose fierce opposition produced a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement that pushed the 2013 Gay Pride onto hotel premises.

Local officials and Pride organisers publicly frame Curaçao, Aruba and Sint Maarten as the drivers of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom, and invoke the island's IGLTA award in promotion of the destination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state which specific offences under the extending Netherlands criminal law would be charged against trans or LGBT people here, the penalties attached, or any case in which they have been used against visitors. No enforcement or prosecution data is available in these sources.

Not sourced in this pass: legal gender recognition, rules for changing sex markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening procedures that could disclose trans status, bathroom and facility rules, hate-crime provisions and their enforcement, and access to gender-affirming medical care on the island.

Whether the April 2015 Kingdom agreement produced legislation inside Curaçao itself is unresolved here. The only documented partner-recognition statute in the subregion is Aruba's of 8 September 2016.

The current operating status and service range of the Pink House centre are not confirmed beyond the January 2017 profile that reported its 2010 opening.
